title: Consolidate Console API aggregation; optimize GraphQL/REST handlers and caching layers
creator: Marco Ruiz
description: Background: The Console backend has accumulated multiple ad-hoc aggregation endpoints and duplicate GraphQL/REST handlers over past releases. This causes inconsistent latency profiles, duplicated DB queries, and brittle cache invalidation paths. Goal: Reduce end-to-end median latency for Console route aggregates by 30%, remove duplicated handler code, and introduce a deterministic two-layer caching strategy (in-process hot cache + Redis TTL cache) with clear invalidation semantics. Scope: identify and consolidate 6 high-traffic aggregation endpoints, refactor GraphQL resolvers to share a central query planner, replace two bespoke caches with a unified caching layer, and add observability (per-route timings, cache hit/miss, miss amplification counters).
acceptance_criteria: Aggregate endpoints consolidated into a single API aggregation module and registered behind existing routes
GraphQL resolvers refactored so shared data-fetching logic is in a single library used by both GraphQL and REST handlers
End-to-end median latency for affected Console pages reduced by >= 30% in staging workload representative of production
Per-route cache hit rate telemetry available in Grafana with alerts for <60% hit rate regression
Automated integration tests validate cache invalidation semantics for create/update/delete flows
No user-facing regressions; smoke tests and canary rollout show zero errors for 48 hours
approach: Phase A: Telemetry and measurement — add route-level timing, DB query counts, and existing cache metrics to identify candidates (2 days)
Phase B: Design consolidation API — define AggregationService interface, consistent input/output shapes, and determinism guarantees (1 day)
Phase C: Refactor resolvers — extract shared fetchers and a lightweight query planner used by both GraphQL resolvers and REST handlers (3 days)
Phase D: Caching layers — implement in-process LRU with per-request TTL and a Redis-backed secondary TTL cache; centralize invalidation hooks (4 days)
Phase E: Integration tests & staging validation — build test harness for invalidation scenarios, run load tests, and iterate on miss amplification fixes (3 days)
Phase F: Canary rollout — 10% traffic for 24h -> 50% for 24h -> 100% if no regressions (2 days)
Phase G: Post-rollout observability tuning and technical debt cleanup (ongoing)
risks: Cache invalidation complexity could cause stale UI data if hooks missed; mitigate with strict tests and short TTLs for high-churn objects
Refactor may introduce subtle GraphQL resolver regressions; mitigate via contract tests between shared fetchers and resolvers
Redis failover could add latency spikes; mitigate by fallback to in-process cache and graceful degradation path
Load test in staging may not perfectly emulate cross-region production traffic patterns
rollout_plan: Merge behind feature flag; deploy to staging and run synthetic smoke + e2e tests
Enable for 10% of Console traffic in production via runtime flag; monitor latency/cpu/cache metrics and error budgets
If stable at 10% for 24h, increase to 50% and re-evaluate; if stable, promote to 100%
If any critical regression detected, flip runtime flag off for immediate rollback
test_plan: Unit tests for AggregationService and shared fetchers
Contract tests ensuring identical GraphQL vs REST responses for same inputs
Integration tests that exercise create/update/delete and assert cache invalidation
Load test (k6) scenario modeled from production traffic traces — compare p50/p95 before/after
Canary e2e smoke tests covering top 5 Console pages
